beats.got: nothing new, just the module title

beats.trigger: A system remembers, grows, and compounds. Chat doesn't.
beats.got: The point is a thing that keeps and improves what it knows, unlike my daily chat use.

beats.trigger: (3) Plan-mode primer. (4) Karpathy's LLM Wiki post.

beats.trigger: See the three layers (raw sources, memory, rules file) and why plain text
beats.got: A list of build skills. Nothing yet about people or roles.

beats.trigger: What's the difference between asking an LLM a question and having an LLM maintain a knowledge base for you?
beats.got: A good question. Chat answers once, and a knowledge base is something that stays and gets looked after.

beats.trigger: If everything you've read and drafted on that challenge moved into a memory an agent could read and sharpen, what changes at work?
beats.got: I can ask this about my own work, like how we onboard people when roles change. That's a leadership-team question.

beats.trigger: The guardrail: propose or draft only, do not send, edit, book, or change anything.
beats.got: A scheduled agent can be kept to drafting only, so a human decides. I could explain that to my works council.

beats.trigger: Scope matters most: a memory about "our company" is a landfill.
beats.got: Pick one narrow challenge and the interview helps me write it down. I'd choose role design through the pricing change.

beats.trigger: Keep it narrow enough that 5–8 topic pages cover it.
beats.got: The next 45 minutes are a build, and I should keep it small.

beats.trigger: Always comply with your company's AI policy.
beats.got: Someone is thinking about data. Good, because I'd normally want people data in here and I shouldn't.

beats.trigger: If the agent starts reading before showing it, stop it, steer narrower, say "continue".
beats.got: Ask for a plan first and keep control of how much it reads.

beats.trigger: Push back, sharpen, add what's missing.
beats.got: The agent proposes sources and I correct it. It feels like briefing a new HR partner.

beats.trigger: List (3), the NOT REACHABLE pile, stays a reference file unless you share it with the agent to save into `sources/`.
beats.got: I couldn't follow the lists (1), (2) and (3) without having seen them. That was jargon.

beats.trigger: Ask the agent to write a plan first and wait for your approval before it touches files.
beats.got: I approve before it acts. That is the same habit I'd want from any team member.

beats.trigger: That list is your first quality check.
beats.got: The agent lists what's weak in its own memory, so I get a to-do list for my own thinking.

beats.trigger: A custom agent is a markdown file of instructions: its purpose and rules.
beats.got: An agent is a page of rules I can read and edit. My HR partners could do that too.

beats.trigger: A good knowledge base sharpens: pages get tighter as new sources arrive, not longer.
beats.got: Adding material made the pages better, not bigger. That is different from my chat history.

beats.trigger: Reject the ones that miss; the agent applies the ones you approve.
beats.got: It suggests fixes and I say yes or no. Fine.

beats.trigger: If the answer is specific and every claim has a citation, the memory works.
beats.got: Citations are how I tell whether it read my files or made it up.

beats.trigger: A system is *persistence* (files it reads again) plus *automation* (it runs).
beats.got: A summary of what I just did. Nothing new.

beats.trigger: The second batch made the first batch better.
beats.got: What I saw in Phase 3 has a name, compounding.

beats.trigger: A saved document with no agent is just a document. An agent with no files is a chat.
beats.got: Files plus an agent is a system. I think "automation" here just means instructions the agent reads, which is not what I'd call automation.

beats.trigger: The existing memory was part of the prompt for updating the memory, so old and new claims met and the ones that couldn't survive got cut.
beats.got: The old pages are fed back in, so weak claims get dropped.

beats.trigger: Keep the rules small and boring.
beats.got: Simple rules, applied again and again. I hear this as how HR policy works too.

beats.trigger: No database, special tool or paid tier is needed.
beats.got: It is just a folder of text anyone can read, which makes it easier to explain and to ask the DPO about.

beats.trigger: Sharpen the memory, never the sources, or you lose the evidence.
beats.got: Keep the originals untouched and let the summaries change. That is good practice for records, too.

beats.trigger: Generic AI becomes your AI when you build the memory it reads.
beats.got: Whoever builds the memory shapes what the AI says, so that ownership is a people question.

beats.trigger: If a competitor could claim a page, the memory is growing but not compounding.
beats.got: A useful test: is this page about us, or about anyone? I can use it on our people strategy.

beats.trigger: Most of what you know about your company sits in heads and corridors, and nobody has written it down.
beats.got: The agent only knows what we write down. That makes knowledge transfer and who writes it a real HR issue, and I can take it to the leadership team.

beats.trigger: The agent writes the rules file from the session: what worked, what rubbed, what got repeated.
beats.got: A retro, then the agent writes the first rules file from it.

beats.trigger: What the agent leaves out is often the signal.
beats.got: Read the summary for what is missing. That is like reading a manager's report.

beats.trigger: Every miss turns into a line of context that stops the next miss.
beats.got: Fix the cause in the rules, not just the one output.

beats.trigger: The model will change under this. The memory will not.
beats.got: What we write down is the lasting asset, not the tool.

beats.trigger: Persistence plus automation: a system.
beats.got: nothing new

beats.trigger: *what is this person automating that they used to do by hand, and what's the move that made it work?*
beats.got: Read three coding practitioners and take notes. They're all engineers, so it's far from my world. Helper agents return a result and disappear, which I only half followed.

beats.trigger: Keep the first version proposal-only: the agent drafts, ranks, or prepares; you decide what leaves the system.

take_homes: An agent only knows what someone wrote down, so the people who write down how we work (onboarding, roles) matter more than I thought. That is a question for my leadership team.
A memory is a plain folder of text with the originals kept untouched, which I can show my HR partners and the DPO without a tool demo.
Make agents propose and a person decide. That is a rule I'd happily put in front of a works council.

monday.move: Write one page on onboarding through the pricing change as my challenge brief, and ask my DPO and the works council contact what employee data may go into an AI tool. No agent build yet.
monday.who: Me, then the DPO and one HR business partner
monday.when: Monday morning for the brief, a call with the DPO by Wednesday
monday.stop_condition: If the DPO says no people data, I keep the memory to policies and public material only.
monday.blocker: Employee data in an AI tool needs the works council and the DPO, and I haven't asked yet.

misconception.why: The module never touched headcount or which roles go. It showed an agent that drafts for a person, which is gentler, but nobody said what it means for jobs, so I leave with my question unanswered.

one_line: Good for seeing why an agent needs a folder of written-down knowledge, but I'd have liked half an hour on what this means for the people doing the work.
